issues.description: The manuscript reports a final analytic sample of N = 372 after exclusions, but the main tables report N = 321 and the moderated model reports N = 244. The transition from 372 to 321 is not explained. This affects interpretation of all analyses, attrition/missingness assessment, power, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: The correlation and mediation tables use N = 321 despite the stated final sample size of N = 372. No explanation is given for excluding 51 additional participants from the main non-moderated analyses.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion due to moderator missingness
issues.description: The moderated regression sample is reduced from the stated final sample of 372 to 244, implying 128 cases were lost for moderation analyses. The extent, pattern, and consequences of this missingness are not adequately addressed, and listwise deletion may bias estimates and reduce power, especially for interaction and conditional indirect effects.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges missing data on perceived patient acuity but does not report the amount of missingness, whether missingness varied by wave, whether missingness was MCAR/MAR, or why imputation/FIML was not used. Dropping many cases for the moderator may bias results and undermines replicability.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.description: Participants who missed a wave were not invited to later waves, creating planned monotone missingness that may amplify attrition bias. The authors provide only a cursory comparison of demographics and broad scale values, without formal attrition analyses or use of longitudinal missing-data methods.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.description: The attrition analysis is informal and insufficient. Reporting that excluded participants were within one standard deviation of included participants does not establish absence of attrition bias; statistical comparisons, effect sizes, and comparisons on all key variables by wave are needed.
issues.quote: Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample of respondents who completed all four time periods – this suggests that the participants who did not complete all time periods were likely not substantially different from those included in the final sample.

issues.description: A large number of participants were excluded for data-quality reasons, especially inconsistent demographics, but the exact rules for 'reasonably consistent' responses are not specified. Such exclusions can introduce bias and analytic flexibility if not transparently preregistered and reproducible.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age)

issues.description: The manuscript states data quality checks were determined a priori but does not report a preregistration, timestamped analysis plan, exact thresholds, or whether hypotheses and models were preregistered. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom in exclusions, variable timing, controls, and supplemental analyses.
issues.quote: Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample.

issues.description: Work hours appear in tables as controls, but the rationale for including them, their timing, and whether they were prespecified are not clearly justified. Control-variable choices can materially alter longitudinal mediation estimates and should be theoretically motivated and consistently reported.

Recruitment materials reportedly required full-time nursing, but the final sample description says all participants were employed part- or full-time. This creates uncertainty about eligibility criteria and sample composition, and part-time status may affect exposure to patient incivility, fatigue, and enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided

issues.subcategory: full-time criterion contradicted by sample description
issues.description: The sample description contradicts the stated inclusion criterion by including part-time nurses. If part-time nurses were included, the study should explain screening, eligibility, and whether work hours were adjusted for exposure opportunities.
issues.quote: All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.description: The study used flyers, personal networks, and social media recruitment, producing a self-selected convenience sample with unknown denominator and response rate. This limits representativeness and increases risk of selection bias, particularly among nurses motivated by incivility or wellbeing concerns.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies...we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks...we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts

issues.subcategory: unknown response rate and sampling frame
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the sampled population size is unknown, preventing calculation of response rates and evaluation of selection bias. This is a major replication and generalizability limitation.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.description: The study aims to sample high-stakes/critical care nurses but relies largely on self-report and only checks O*Net alignment for 20 randomly selected participants. This does not verify that the full analytic sample met inclusion criteria, especially given broad recruitment through social media and MTurk pilot procedures.
issues.quote: In addition, we reviewed the O*Net job descriptions for a randomly selected group of n = 20 participants.

issues.description: Patient acuity is defined as severity of illness and intensity of nursing care required, but is measured with one self-reported percentage of patients considered 'severe' across heterogeneous departmental scales. This conflates objective acuity, perceived workload, patient mix, departmental norms, and respondent interpretation, weakening construct validity of the moderator.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: The acuity item invites respondents to use different departmental scales with different scoring systems and clinical meanings. A percentage classified as 'severe' under ESI, CRIB, SOIS, or other tools may not be comparable across specialties, threatening measurement invariance and validity.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools

issues.description: Patient acuity, a central moderator, is measured with a single newly developed item. Reliability cannot be assessed, and measurement error likely attenuates or distorts interaction estimates. The item also produced substantial invalid or missing responses, suggesting comprehension or applicability problems.
issues.quote: To develop our perceived patient acuity measure, we first discussed patient acuity measurement strategies...we tested this new item within the quantitative pilot study.

issues.subcategory: invalid acuity responses indicate measurement failure
issues.description: Nearly half of missing acuity values were responses outside the expected numeric range, indicating participants misunderstood the item or response format. This raises concerns about validity even among retained responses.
issues.quote: 45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response

issues.description: The theoretical argument emphasizes compassion fatigue as caregiving burnout plus secondary trauma, but the hypothesized mediator is driven by patient incivility and negative emotions toward patients. Incivility does not necessarily involve exposure to trauma or suffering, so the construct may partly capture general burnout/distress rather than compassion fatigue as defined.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.subcategory: shortened incivility scales and content coverage
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility were assessed using four selected items from longer scales. Although some pilot justification is provided, item selection based on highest loadings may narrow the construct and overemphasize overt disrespect while omitting other incivility facets. This may affect comparability with prior WIS findings.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability

issues.subcategory: self-reported enacted mistreatment susceptible to bias
issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is measured solely by self-report. Because admitting patient mistreatment is socially undesirable and potentially professionally sensitive, estimates may be biased, and common-source associations with negative emotions and fatigue may be inflated.
issues.quote: Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale (Cortina et al., 2001) were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.description: All substantive variables are self-reported by the same respondent. Temporal spacing helps but does not remove common method, affective, social desirability, and negative response-style biases, especially given extremely high correlations among constructs.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: extremely high correlations and discriminant validity concerns
issues.description: Correlations among theoretically distinct constructs are extremely high, e.g., T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility r = .94, T3 negative emotions and T4 enacted incivility r = .87, and T2 customer incivility and T4 compassion fatigue r = .85. These values suggest severe overlap/common-method bias or lack of discriminant validity, undermining mediation interpretation.

The CFA results omit the chi-square symbol for the hypothesized model and report comparison models with only parenthetical numbers that appear to be degrees of freedom or chi-square differences. Degrees of freedom, chi-square values, model comparisons, and factor correlations are inadequately and inconsistently reported, preventing evaluation of discriminant validity.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor (3) = 82.52, RMSEA = .09, CFI = .98, TLI = .98)

issues.description: The one-, two-, and three-factor CFA models have nearly identical excellent CFI/TLI values despite very high intercorrelations and only small reported test values. The reporting appears inconsistent or erroneous, and the evidence does not convincingly establish discriminant validity.
issues.quote: a two-factor model... (2) = 82.65, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), and a one-factor model (1) = 8.02, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98).

issues.subcategory: CFA excludes temporal controls and possibly repeated measures structure
issues.description: The CFA is conducted 'absent of the temporal control measures' and apparently ignores repeated measures across waves. It is unclear which wave(s) were included and whether nonindependence and longitudinal measurement invariance were assessed. This limits claims of discriminant validity across time.
issues.quote: First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures.

issues.description: Because the same constructs are measured over four waves and autoregressive paths are modeled, longitudinal measurement invariance should be tested or justified. Without it, changes and lagged relationships may reflect changes in measurement properties over time.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: autoregressive model not clearly implemented in tables
issues.description: The analytic strategy claims to model AR(1) paths and covariances among variables within waves, but the regression tables do not show lagged same-variable controls for negative emotions, compassion fatigue, or enacted incivility. It is unclear whether baseline and autoregressive controls were actually included in hypothesis tests.
issues.quote: This allowed us to assess stability over time by modeling the autocorrelations (AR1) between each variable and its prior occasions and the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave

issues.description: The model is described only generally. The manuscript does not provide full path specifications, all covariances, residual correlations, estimator for structural models, handling of missingness, exact software syntax, or whether paths were constrained/equated over time. This prevents replication.
issues.quote: we assessed each variable during each wave. This allowed us to assess stability over time by modeling the autocorrelations (AR1) between each variable and its prior occasions and the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave

issues.subcategory: same-wave mediator-outcome path in serial mediation
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 is described as longitudinal serial mediation, but compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both measured at T4. The path from compassion fatigue to enacted incivility is contemporaneous, not temporally ordered, weakening causal mediation claims and making reverse causation plausible.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: same-time mediator and outcome in table
issues.description: The mediation table confirms that compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both at T4, yet the paper interprets this as a serial process unfolding over time. Same-wave assessment cannot establish that compassion fatigue precedes enacted incivility.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | .57*** | .17 | 3.35

issues.subcategory: overstated causal language from observational data
issues.description: The study is observational, self-report, and nonexperimental, yet uses causal wording such as 'leads to' and 'effect.' Temporal precedence is partial and confounding remains possible, so causal claims are not warranted.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: The manuscript claims stronger causal inference from autoregressive mediation, but such models do not eliminate confounding by stable traits, workplace climate, unit-level stressors, negative affectivity, leadership, staffing ratios, shift type, or patient population. Without randomization or stronger quasi-experimental controls, causal interpretation remains limited.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects...and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.description: Negative affectivity, trait anger, burnout proneness, conscientiousness, empathy, and social desirability could influence reports of experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility. The analyses do not appear to control for stable between-person confounding or use within-person fixed effects.
issues.quote: using a single source can raise concerns associated with common method variance

issues.description: Hospital unit, staffing, leadership, patient-to-nurse ratios, shift length, night work, specialty, and organizational civility climate may cause both patient incivility and nurse fatigue/enacted incivility. Recruitment across unknown hospitals and units without clustering or controls leaves these confounds unresolved.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S.

issues.description: Participants are likely nested within hospitals, units, and recruitment networks, but the analyses treat observations as independent. Shared environments could inflate precision and confound estimates, particularly for incivility and acuity.
issues.quote: First, we dropped off recruitment flyers with the study information at three hospitals local to the research team.

issues.subcategory: mediation inference with omitted direct/alternative paths
issues.description: The serial mediation model assumes a specific causal ordering but does not report testing plausible reverse or reciprocal paths, such as enacted incivility predicting later experienced incivility, compassion fatigue predicting later negative emotions, or baseline levels predicting change. Given high correlations, reciprocal models are important.
issues.quote: we examine both emotional response and exhaustion mechanisms and examine the sequential mediation pathway from stressor to emotion to compassion fatigue to CWB over time.

issues.description: The text reports the serial indirect effect as B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]. A coefficient of .06 with SE .04 would not normally yield p < .01, and the CI width is more consistent with a smaller SE. Table 2 reports SE = .02 for the same indirect effect. This inconsistency suggests reporting or calculation error.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: indirect effect SE differs between text and table
issues.description: The same serial indirect effect is reported with SE = .04 in the text and SE = .02 in Table 2. This affects statistical significance and confidence in the result.
issues.quote: Customer Incivility  Negative Emotions  Compassion Fatigue  Enacted Incivility | .06** | .02 | 2.58

issues.description: For several indirect effects and simple slopes, p-values and confidence intervals are both reported, but it is unclear whether p-values are derived from normal theory, Monte Carlo intervals, or model constraints. For indirect effects, normal-theory p-values may be inappropriate given asymmetric product distributions.
issues.quote: We then used a Monte Carlo simulation with 20,000 replications...to construct confidence intervals around the parameter estimates of all indirect effects and the Index of Moderated Mediation (IMM).

issues.description: The relative importance analysis is described as each predictor accounting for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility. These percentages likely refer to proportions of explained variance, not total variance, and the analysis uses predictors highly collinear with one another, making interpretation unstable. It also appears inconsistent with the preceding table coefficients.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: relative importance coefficients inconsistent with Table 2
issues.description: The supplemental regression reports compassion fatigue B = .23 and negative emotions B = .23, whereas Table 2 reports compassion fatigue B = .57 and negative emotions B = .28 in the enacted incivility equation. The difference may reflect a different model, but this is not explained.
issues.quote: we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.description: Table 3 has duplicated/misaligned columns and unclear coefficient placement, making it difficult to determine which coefficients correspond to which dependent variables. This undermines interpretability and reproducibility.
issues.quote: | B | SE | t | B | B | SE | t | B | B | SE | t | B | SE | t

issues.description: Table 3 reports negative emotions predicting enacted incivility as B = .35 with SE = .11 and t = 3.14 but no significance stars in one row, despite t = 3.14 typically corresponding to p < .01. This suggests table formatting or reporting errors.

The text reports the main effect of T2 experienced incivility on T3 negative emotions as B = .26 in the simple model and the moderated model as medium slope B = .22. Table 3 also shows duplicated B values and confusing entries, making it unclear whether the moderation model was correctly specified and reported.
issues.quote: Results revealed that the Time 2 experienced incivility × Time 2 perceived patient acuity interaction term was significant (B = .34, SE = .12, p < .01).

issues.description: The enacted incivility model reports R2 = .81 and correlations with compassion fatigue near .94. Such high explanatory power among self-report constructs measured contemporaneously suggests common method overlap or redundancy rather than substantive prediction, and requires careful diagnostic reporting.

Incivility enactment is likely skewed and socially sensitive, but the manuscript treats Likert composite scores as continuous normal outcomes and does not report distributions, floor/ceiling effects, or robust checks. Violated assumptions could affect regression and mediation estimates.
issues.quote: Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always).

issues.description: No a priori power analysis or precision justification is reported for mediation, moderated mediation, or interaction effects. This is especially important because the moderator sample is only N = 244 and conditional indirect effects are typically underpowered.
issues.quote: Data were collected at four time points across four consecutive weeks

issues.description: The moderated mediation analysis is conducted on N = 244 due to missing acuity data, and the conditional indirect effects are nonsignificant. Without power analysis, the study cannot distinguish absence of moderated mediation from insufficient power.
issues.quote: Interestingly, our expectations were not supported as the slopes at low...medium...and high levels...of perceived patient acuity were all non-significant.

issues.description: Hypothesis 3 states moderation of experienced incivility to negative emotions, but the results section says it predicted moderation of the first stage of the relationship between experienced incivility and compassion fatigue. This conflates the simple and mediated models and may confuse the intended moderated mediation.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 3 predicted that the first stage of the relationship (experienced incivility related to negative emotions towards patients) between experienced incivility and compassion fatigue would be moderated by perceived patient acuity.

issues.description: The paper alternates among customers, patients, and patient family members/friends. Patients and families differ in role, vulnerability, autonomy, and source of incivility. Combining them may obscure distinct processes and weakens construct specificity.
issues.quote: the customers are the patients and their families. The incivility examined is therefore incivility from patients and their families (experienced incivility) and incivility towards patients and their families (enacted incivility).

issues.description: The manuscript treats nurse-patient relationships as a specialized customer-employee relationship, but clinical care relationships are ethically, legally, and structurally distinct from typical customer service. The theoretical implications for 'customer incivility' may not transfer straightforwardly.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship.

issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly female, predominantly White, self-selected, and limited to nurses in high-stakes/high-risk settings. The manuscript sometimes generalizes to service employees and service industries broadly, which exceeds the sampling frame.
issues.quote: Using a four-wave data collection of service employees within the healthcare industry

issues.description: The conclusion extrapolates from high-stakes nurses to customers and service industries generally. Healthcare settings involve unique stressors, ethical obligations, patient vulnerability, and team-based care, limiting generalizability.
issues.quote: experiencing customer incivility (a common occurrence within the service industries)

issues.subcategory: no blinding possible and demand characteristics
issues.description: Participants knew the study concerned work experiences, wellbeing, and success and repeatedly completed identical surveys. Repeated self-report measurement may increase hypothesis guessing, consistency motifs, and demand characteristics, especially for morally loaded enacted incivility.
issues.quote: The purpose of the study is to investigate the influence of work experiences on employee wellbeing and success.

issues.subcategory: survey timing and exposure windows unclear
issues.description: The manuscript uses weekly retrospective reports but does not report when surveys were completed relative to shifts, number of shifts worked, whether respondents worked during each interval, or how overlapping recall windows were handled. This matters for exposure to patients, incivility, acuity, and fatigue.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.description: Nurses varied in work hours and likely number of shifts/patients, but patient counts and exposure opportunities were not measured. Work hours are included inconsistently and cannot substitute for number/type of patient interactions, which affects both experienced and enacted incivility.
issues.quote: we did not ask them to report on the specific assessment used, number of patients seen in that week, or the number of patients that were actually classified as severe within their assessment tool.

issues.description: Only selected wave variables are shown in Table 1, despite all constructs reportedly measured at all four waves. Means, SDs, reliabilities, and correlations for all waves are needed to evaluate stability, attrition, and longitudinal modeling.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents intercorrelations among study variables and descriptive information.

issues.subcategory: Cronbach alpha for omitted waves not reported
issues.description: Reliabilities are reported only for variables appearing in Table 1. Because the same scales are used repeatedly and time-specific measures enter different parts of the model, reliability across all waves should be reported.
issues.quote: Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.description: The manuscript adapted wording from customer to patient/patient family members and shortened scales, but does not report full pilot psychometrics, factor loadings, item response distributions, or evidence that adapted enacted incivility items function equivalently in healthcare contexts.
issues.quote: Because of the healthcare sample, the word “customer” was replaced with “patient” or “patient or patient family members/friends” for any scales that asked about customer interactions.

issues.subcategory: pilot sample from MTurk may not verify clinical relevance
issues.description: The quantitative pilot of high-stakes nurses recruited from MTurk may have uncertain occupational verification. This limits the strength of pilot evidence for adapted healthcare measures unless verification procedures are reported.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.

issues.description: Patient acuity is described as a percentage, but Table 1 reports means around .52, suggesting proportions. The manuscript does not clearly state whether percentages were transformed to proportions before analysis, which is necessary to interpret coefficients such as B = .34 for the interaction.
issues.quote: T2 Patient Acuity | .52 | .28

issues.subcategory: confidence intervals omitted for main paths
issues.description: Most regression paths are reported with B, SE, and p but without confidence intervals. For longitudinal mediation and moderation, CIs for all key paths and indirect effects would improve interpretability and reproducibility.
issues.quote: experienced patient incivility was positively related to negative emotions toward patients (B = .26, SE = .06, p < .001).

issues.description: The manuscript reports B coefficients but does not clearly state whether they are unstandardized or standardized. This is important because variables use different scales, and interaction/simple slope interpretation depends on metric and centering.
issues.quote: Predictors in the moderated mediation model were centered at their respective grand means.

issues.subcategory: temporal separation insufficient for mediation claims
issues.description: Although variables are measured weekly, the proposed psychological process from incivility to emotions to fatigue to enactment may occur within hours or days. Weekly lags may miss or conflate the actual causal timing, and same-week retrospective reports can include events occurring after the supposed mediator/outcome.
issues.quote: Data were collected at four time points across four consecutive weeks, with each survey administered one week apart

issues.subcategory: identical weekly surveys may induce panel conditioning
issues.description: Administering identical surveys weekly can sensitize participants to incivility and emotions, potentially changing reporting or behavior. The manuscript does not discuss panel conditioning.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.subcategory: patient acuity moderation inconsistent with moderated mediation conclusion
issues.description: The manuscript emphasizes patient acuity as exacerbating detrimental relationships and practical risk, but the conditional indirect effect and IMM are nonsignificant. Claims that acuity worsens the overall downstream pathway to enacted incivility are not supported.
issues.quote: Taken together, these results reveal the indirect effect is not conditional upon perceived patient acuity.

issues.subcategory: discussion overstates moderation beyond supported path
issues.description: The discussion says nurses with high incivility and high patient acuity are at highest risk of negative affect, fatigue, and ultimately incivility, but the moderated mediation was nonsignificant. Only the incivility-to-negative-emotions path was moderated.
issues.quote: Together, our results suggest that employees experiencing incivility from patients and who have a high perceived patient acuity load are at the highest risk of experiencing increased negative affect and fatigue and, ultimately, engaging in incivility.

issues.description: The paper recommends identifying employees with high incivility and developing interventions to stop the process, but the observational design cannot establish that reducing patient incivility or targeting affect/fatigue will reduce enacted incivility.
issues.quote: Organizations should identify who is experiencing high levels of incivility and develop support systems and interventions for these employees to stop the negative affective and energetic process our results suggest are occurring.

issues.subcategory: no correction or plan for multiple testing
issues.description: The study tests multiple paths, indirect effects, moderation, conditional indirect effects, supplemental relative importance analyses, and model comparisons without a stated multiplicity plan. This increases false-positive risk, especially for exploratory supplemental analyses.
issues.quote: We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.description: Supplemental analyses are not clearly labeled as exploratory in terms of preregistration status, and the relative importance findings are used to make substantive theoretical claims about compassion fatigue being a stronger driver. This may capitalize on chance.
issues.quote: Further, our results suggest that while the emotion response is an important proximal response to incivility experiences, the subsequent compassion fatigue response is a stronger driver of enacted incivility.

issues.description: The manuscript refers to Figures 1–3 but provides no figure content beyond captions in the supplied text. The model and results cannot be fully evaluated, especially given table formatting problems.
issues.quote: see Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from

issues.subcategory: correlation table signs unexpected and unexplained
issues.description: Work hours are strongly negatively correlated with incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility (around -.35 to -.44). This counterintuitive pattern may indicate coding, sampling, or data-quality issues and is not discussed despite work hours being used as a control.

issues.subcategory: data-quality exclusion details insufficient for duplicate detection
issues.description: The duplicate-response exclusion criterion is vague. It is unclear what open-ended attention checks were used, how similarity was assessed, whether IP/device/time stamps were used, and whether participants were excluded across all waves or only specific responses.
issues.quote: duplicate responses (identical content, syntax, and formatting) to open ended attention check questions as other participants (suggesting repeat survey participation and/or collusion) (n = 21).

issues.description: The open online recruitment with gift cards and no participant emails obtained during recruitment increases risk of duplicate/fraudulent participation. The large number of data-quality exclusions suggests this occurred, but prevention and verification procedures are insufficiently described.
issues.quote: Participants received a $5 gift card for each survey they completed (with a possible $20 total earned).

issues.description: The manuscript does not report institutional review board approval, informed consent procedures beyond recruitment materials, confidentiality protections, or handling of sensitive admissions of patient mistreatment. This is important given healthcare workers reporting uncivil behavior toward patients.
issues.quote: The study information included in the recruitment fliers stated: “The purpose of the study is to investigate the influence of work experiences on employee wellbeing and success.”

issues.subcategory: negative emotions toward all patients after incivility from some patients
issues.description: The negative-emotion measure asks about emotions toward patients generally, whereas experienced incivility may come from patients or family members/friends. This generalization across targets may be theoretically plausible, but it also conflates emotions toward perpetrators, nonperpetrating patients, and families.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to rate “How often do you feel the following emotions towards patients”

issues.subcategory: experienced incivility source includes family but mediator omits family
issues.description: Experienced incivility includes patients and family/friends, but negative emotions are measured toward patients only. If much incivility comes from family members, the mediator does not match the source of the stressor.
issues.quote: how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends…

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility target includes family but construct label says patients
issues.description: The enacted incivility items refer to patients/patient family members, but the construct is labeled enacted incivility toward patients. This imprecision matters because incivility toward family members may have different antecedents and implications than incivility toward patients.
issues.quote: Put down one or more patients/patient family members or acted condescendingly towards them

issues.subcategory: mislabeling chronic exposure with four weekly measures
issues.description: The manuscript frames incivility as chronic/cumulative, but measures only four weekly retrospective reports and primarily tests adjacent lagged paths. This limited window may not capture chronic exposure or accumulation as conceptually described.
issues.quote: how cumulative weekly exposure to incivility across customers and workdays can influence employee wellbeing and behaviors.

issues.subcategory: no modeling of cumulative exposure despite claims
issues.description: Although the theory emphasizes cumulative exposure, the hypothesis tests use T2 incivility predicting T3/T4 outcomes rather than cumulative, growth, average exposure, or latent trajectory models. The analysis does not directly test accumulation.
issues.quote: We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).

issues.subcategory: results claim four-wave survey but hypotheses use subset of waves
issues.description: The abstract and discussion emphasize four-wave longitudinal evidence, but the primary reported paths use T2, T3, and T4, with T1 only as an unclear baseline control. This is not wrong, but the use of all four waves should be transparently specified.
issues.quote: Results from the four-wave survey indicate that experienced patient incivility is positively related to negative emotions and to compassion fatigue

issues.description: The text says T1 variables were modeled as baseline controls, but the reported tables do not show T1 control coefficients or explain why they are omitted. Readers cannot verify whether effects are change-adjusted.
